name: Marín
title: Marín Ship Gauging | UTM Thickness Measurement, Pontevedra
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging at Marín on the Ría de Pontevedra: timber and bulk carriers, steel cargo, fishing vessels and tugs, hull and tank UTM.
h1: Marín (Pontevedra) Ship Thickness Gauging for Bulk, Timber and Fishing Vessels
intro: Marín is the commercial port of the Ría de Pontevedra, a working harbour for timber, steel and bulk cargo, a large fishing fleet and a naval school that gives the town its other identity. It lies a short distance from Vigo's yards. Our ultrasonic thickness gauging technicians travel from India to the ship, measuring hold structure, tanks and shell at the quay or at anchor.

highlights.p: Log carriers and steel cargo vessels load at Marín, and both punish holds and coamings. Gauging during loading and discharge pauses concentrates on frames, tank tops and hatch edges.
Marín has a substantial fishing harbour and craft yards. Hull and tank readings on trawlers and tugs support refit decisions, usually taken alongside before a vessel moves to a larger yard.

highlights.h: A short step from Vigo's docks
highlights.p: Readings taken at Marín feed straight into dockings at the yards in Vigo, a short passage across the ría system, with the same technicians available to return once the ship is dry.

port.h: A working port on the Ría de Pontevedra
p: Marín lies on the northern shore of the Ría de Pontevedra, one of the Galician rías, sheltered by the island of Ons and the peninsula of O Morrazo. The port is a specialist commercial harbour rather than a general gateway, with berths designed for bulk, timber and steel, and next to them a fishing quay and boat-building area where small and medium vessels are built and repaired. The water in the ría is deep enough for ocean-going bulk carriers at the main quays, and the sheltered setting means weather rarely stops work for long.

Timber is the port's signature cargo. Galicia is one of Europe's major forestry regions, and Marín ships logs and wood products on bulk carriers and general cargo vessels, some of them with deck cargoes that demand careful stowage and lashing. Steel products, cereals, fertiliser and other bulk cargoes move through the same berths, and some cargoes arrive for the pulp and wood-processing industries that surround the ría. The fishing harbour handles trawlers and coastal boats and supplies the fish-processing trade, while the naval school, a major training establishment for Spain's navy, adds its own small craft to the harbour scene.

These trades shape the inspection work. Timber and steel loading punish cargo holds, with frames, tank top plating and hatch coamings suffering impact damage and abrasion, and deck cargoes can load the structure unevenly. Older bulk and general cargo ships that have worked the northern European timber trade for years are common candidates for a condition check. Fishing vessels and tugs bring different issues, such as wastage in tanks and at the waterline, while owners of the smaller ships tend to prefer gauging alongside at Marín rather than detouring to a yard for survey-only work.

Marín has no large commercial drydock, so heavy work normally goes to Vigo, a short passage away by sea, where floating docks and repair quays take merchant and fishing ships. At Marín itself, ships are gauged alongside at the main commercial berths, at the timber and steel quays, in the fishing harbour or at the anchorage in the ría. Holds are available once cargo is cleared, ballast tanks whenever the chief officer can release them and the enclosed-space permit is in place, and the shell at the waterline wherever staging or a work boat gives safe access.

The local craft and boat-building yards handle small repairs, and fishing vessels hauled there for maintenance can be gauged out of the water at the slipway when the owner agrees. For merchant ships, the usual pattern is to measure at Marín, fix the steel list and send it to the yard that will do the work. Where a ship waits at anchor for a berth, a launch from the agent allows readings in empty holds and ballast tanks, and the sheltered ría makes boarding more reliable than on open-coast anchorages.
list: Commercial berths — hold frame, tank top and hatch coaming gauging on bulk and general cargo ships
Timber and steel quays — deck, coaming and ballast tank readings on log carriers and steel cargo vessels
Fishing harbour quays — hull and tank gauging on trawlers and coastal fishing boats
Boat-yard slipways — shell and bottom readings on fishing vessels and tugs hauled for maintenance
Ría anchorage — launch-served gauging of empty holds and ballast tanks on ships waiting for a berth
Pre-docking steel lists for onward yards at Vigo or elsewhere on the Galician coast

context.h: Oversight and obligations around the ría
p: Port state control at Marín falls under the Paris MoU, carried out by the Spanish maritime administration, the Dirección General de la Marina Mercante, through the local Capitanía Marítima. The port sees fewer foreign-flag deep-sea calls than its neighbour Vigo, but bulk and general cargo ships of varied age come for timber and steel, and some are chosen for inspection. A superintendent who has had the holds and ballast tanks measured before arrival can address any thinning before an inspector finds it, which keeps the loading programme on schedule.

EU rules add their own drivers. European recycling rules want a current Inventory of Hazardous Materials aboard ships entering EU ports, the carbon market has covered shipping since 2024 and FuelEU Maritime has applied since 2025, and all of this push owners to know their fleet's condition when deciding on retrofit, sale or retirement. For timber carriers, cargo securing and deck loading add safety obligations that make sound hatch covers and coamings important, and gauging those items before a loading is a practical way to reduce the risk of a claim.

jobs.p: Marín's jobs are led by cargo ships loading timber, steel and other bulk, and by fishing and small-craft owners. The superintendent sends the survey status and the compartments of concern, we confirm what the cargo plan allows, and the technicians travel from India once the stay is confirmed. A coordinated plan between the quay and the yard in Vigo is common. Typical requests include:
list: Hold frame, tank top and hatch coaming gauging on a log carrier between voyages, to assess impact damage and abrasion from timber handling.
Ballast tank and deck gauging on a steel cargo ship before its intermediate survey, completed while the holds are being prepared for the next load.
Shell and ballast tank readings on a fishing vessel hauled at a local slipway, to size steel renewal before refit.
Condition gauging of an older general cargo ship for a buyer, covering holds, hatch covers and ballast tanks, completed at the quay before the sale proceeds.
A pre-docking steel list taken on a small bulk carrier at the ría anchorage, sent to a yard in Vigo ahead of the dock slot.

logistics: Technicians usually reach Marín through Vigo-Peinador or Santiago de Compostela airport, with road transfers around the ría, connecting through Madrid or Lisbon on the way from India. The ship's agent arranges port passes and launch boats for the anchorage. Spain belongs to the Schengen area, so each technician needs a visa obtained in India, applied for once the stay is confirmed and supported by an invitation naming the vessel. Cargo plans change often, so travel is booked as late as the visa process allows.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock at Marín?
faqs.a: Not for large merchant ships. Heavy repairs normally go to Vigo, a short distance away, where floating docks and repair quays are available. We measure at Marín, alongside or at anchor, and prepare the steel list so the yard can plan the docking from actual plate thickness.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged on a timber carrier at Marín?
faqs.a: Yes, once cargo has been discharged and the holds are safe to enter. We concentrate on frames, tank top plating, hatch coamings and the lower side shell, which take the most abuse from timber handling. If cargo is being loaded the same day, we agree a gap in operations with the chief officer.

faqs.q: Can you gauge fishing vessels at Marín?
faqs.a: Yes. Trawlers and coastal fishing boats are measured at the quay or on a local slipway when hauled out. We pay attention to fish holds, ballast and fuel tanks, the shell at the waterline and areas rubbed by gear, and report compartment by compartment for the owner's refit planning.

faqs.q: Does the naval school affect commercial gauging?
faqs.a: The naval school is a separate establishment with its own berths and rules, and commercial work does not take place there. It adds small craft to the harbour area, but access to the commercial quays and the fishing harbour is arranged through the ship's agent and the port in the usual way.
